title: "Caregivers’ fake news detection ability predicts vaccine confidence and uptake of childhood immunizations"
author: "Yongjin Choi (LSHTM, Yongjin.Choi@lshtm.ac.uk)"
date: today
abstract: |
  **Background.** Exposure to misinformation has been linked to false beliefs that can shape political attitudes and adversely impact health outcomes, such as adoption of health interventions, including vaccines. Previous work has linked exposure to misinformation and the ability to identify fake news, but less is known about how individuals’ misinformation susceptibility links to vaccine confidence more broadly and plausibly impacts population-level uptake rates of childhood immunisations. We examined these relationships among caregivers and assessed whether they differed by political orientation.

  **Methods.** We quantified caregivers’ susceptibility to misinformation using the 20-item Misinformation Susceptibility Test, administered in cross-sectional surveys of 14,555 caregivers of children in 2025 -- in the US (n=12,555), the UK (n=1000), and Canada (n=1000). We fitted Bayesian two-parameter logistic item response models to the fake- and real-news items separately, yielding individual-level estimates of ability to detect fake news, real news, and related response tendencies, while accounting for item-level differences and uncertainty in individual ability estimates. We then examined how these abilities related to caregivers’ vaccine confidence, political orientation, childhood MCV uptake, and whether the associations with vaccine confidence differed by political orientation. We also built a counterfactual model of MCV uptake to examine how differences in headline detection could translate into differences in vaccination uptake through vaccine confidence.

  **Results.** Caregivers better able to identify fake news headlines reported higher vaccine confidence in all three countries and across all five vaccine confidence outcomes. In the US, a 1 standard deviation (SD) increase in fake-news detection ability corresponded to odds ratios of 1.40-1.72 (all 95% CIs excluded 1; P<0.0001). Each additional correctly rejected headline corresponded to a 1.7-2.3 percentage point higher predicted probability of vaccine confidence. Associations were also positive in the UK and Canada, although estimates were less precise. Real-news detection was also associated with vaccine confidence but more weakly in the US. Fake-news detection was lower among politically conservative caregivers in all three countries, particularly in the US and Canada. Counterfactual projections indicated higher MCV uptake at higher levels of fake-news detection in all three countries.

  **Implication.** Vaccine attitudes reflect not only what caregivers know about vaccines but how well they can distinguish reliable information from misinformation. Caregiver decision-making determines health outcomes for their children: differences in caregiver discernment become not just a question of differences in cognitive traits, but a question of equity in child health. The association between fake-news headline detection, vaccine confidence, and projected MCV uptake suggests that misinformation susceptibility may be a modifiable pathway of public-health importance. Interventions strengthening caregivers’ information discernment are needed alongside efforts to depoliticise vaccines, particularly where these pressures are most acute, such as the USA, where exemptions to childhood vaccines have hit a record high.

::: {.fig-note}
*Note.* Markers on the X-axis are odds ratios estimated from country-specific multilevel models, while horizontal lines indicate 95% CIs. Odds ratios are per 1 SD increase in detection score. The dashed line marks the null (odds ratio 1). Models used post-stratification weights and adjusted for sociodemographic covariates, perceived ease of access to and affordability of vaccination, and first-level administrative region. Samples comprise 11,380 respondents in the USA, 946 in the UK, and 920 in Canada.
:::
